utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there was a preliminary matter but very short if I understand well, so meanwhile perhaps we could already -- if it's about the replacement of a translation. Then could the witness already be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Bibles, could I just try to anticipate on what you would like to do, that is, to replace the translation which is now attached to P01968 by an improved -- by a revised English translation which was admitted in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the new 65 ter number for the translation which replaces the old one would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- this English translation was not on the 65 ter list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- so it will be a straight replacement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Straight replacement. You have uploaded it into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's being uploaded right now. It will be available in about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Registrar is instructed to replace the existing English translation of P01968 with the revised translation. Mr. Lukic, if there would be any reason to re-visit the matter, you have an opportunity to do so within the next 48 hours. Good morning, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not very polite to address other matters while you enter the courtroom, but apologies for that. Mr. Donia, I would like to remind you, as I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you, as I did before, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar informs me that you would like to address the Chamber on a matter which arose yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would, Your Honour. If you would be so kind as to give me perhaps two or three minutes. This is in response to a series of questions that you asked me at the very end of the session which I feel I did not adequately answer. So I would like to try and have another run at it by offering two considerations. Number one: I think that your question kind of caught me in a position between two worlds. As a historian, I feel that my obligation and work is intended to observe, explicate, and in some sense analyse human behaviour rather than to judge it. And the question that you -- first question that you raised me -- in fact, Mr. Lukic asked, is really a question of the judgement, namely, was the -- was the -- was fear justified on the part of the Bosnian Serbs at this time. The second consideration I would offer is that there really is, I think, a kind of bifurcated answer to this question. It goes right to the heart of the position that I outlined at the very beginning of my testimony; namely, my view of ethnicity and identity, and specifically the character of groupness, if any, that pertains to peoples, not just the Serbs, but Croats, Muslims, and others. And as I think about this, the Bosnian Serbs really -- the leaders at least lived in a world in which they conceptualised the Serb people as a singular entity, as a living, bounded, defined thing with substance and definition. And my view with that is that's -- that would be something to be proven rather than simply assumed. But I think if you believe that the Serb people exists in this sense, that then naturally it has rights and those rights can be respected or violated in this way of looking at things. And I think the answer to the question is: If you believed that the Serb people really is this bounded, firm, solid entity, then the Serb people as such will experience fear and justifiable fear because it is the Serb people's existence as this entity that is threatened. On the other hand, if you look empirically at the behaviour of individuals, including those leaders of the group at this time, I don't see any evidence that they were experiencing or reflecting -- they weren't engaging in any fearful behaviour. They were rather doing what most political groups do when they are out-voted. They go back to the drawing boards, they mobilise, they seek to get more voters and more votes next time, they sharpen their arguments, and they take a different tactical approach. So my answer to the question of whether individuals who may identify with this broader collectivity, in fact, experience fear at this time, I do not see evidence that they did. Thank you, that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That is a rather confusing line of questions and answer about fear being justified. You could put the question: Is fear for thunderstorms justified? There may be no real answer to that. What you can do is you can analyse. First of all, you can establish that someone experiences fear, that's one; second, you can ask yourself whether there are objective reasons in the past or in the present which would explain why people become fearful under certain circumstances. I leave it to that, but I think from an analytical point of view - and you have -- although you again talked about justified fear, as the question was about justified fear, whereas an analytical approach would seek explanations on the basis of experiences and that is apparently what you added in the second part of your answer you gave today. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was trying to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Lukic, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good morning, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am just going to add something to what you told us this morning. You dealt with some excerpts here from the Assembly. Was there a fear of genocide among the Serb people at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] You're asking me to assume that the Serb people experience these feelings, and it's difficult for me to jump into that world. I think that I could say that many Serbs have been persuaded to fear a recurrence of genocide by the constant drum-beat of references to historical genocide on the part of the leaders, intellectual and political, of the Bosnian Serb movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Already at that time the Serbs in Croatia had lost the status of a people; right? They were proclaimed a national minority and in the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia at that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that's a distinction in Yugoslav socialist nationality theory, that this is kind of unrecognisable to most other people, most people outside of Yugoslavia. But within the -- accepting the definitions of those terms as they existed in socialist political thought, Yugoslav socialist political thought, that's correct. They had been, say, recharacterised from being a constituent people to being a minority, which is in that Yugoslav system a demotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Serbs or at least Serb politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina tried to avoid that descent, if you will, in terms of status, that is to say to be demoted from the status of a people to a status of a minority, and does that affect the rights that a certain group of people enjoy in a certain state, first and foremost, in Yugoslavia, the state that they lived in before that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sense two somewhat different questions here. Let me address the first one first. I know of no effort that was made on the part of other political forces, other political factions, in Bosnia to demote the Serbs from the status of a constituent nation to a minority. I don't believe that that was, at least not seriously, proposed by anyone. It wasn't really a part of the political conversation. It may be that the interpretation of Serb politicians was that these acts amounted to ignoring the constituent status of the Serbs, but there was, to my knowledge, no effort to ever demote them, as had happened in Croatia and therefore no opposition to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that through out-voting, simple out-voting and the loss of status by not being a constituent people anymore, would the Serbs, in fact, become a minority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think, you know, out-voting happens every day in every democratic system. Part of living in a democratic state is losing once in a while, and the meaning of this term that the Serbs assigned to it was I think part of this internal lexical convention that prevailed within the Bosnian Serb movement that assigned to this notion of losing a vote, a far greater, in fact, constitutional significance than it actually had. And I don't think that losing a vote or even a lot of votes necessarily translates into converting a people, a "narod," into a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time the divisions in Bosnia were not democratic, they went along ethnic lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there -- no, I don't think that's correct. They were democratic in the sense that they were the result of voting and the results of voting or they were a product of voting. The -- not only the constitution but the way in which electoral districts were held -- elections were held gave some weight to the ethnicity of the voter as he or she self-identified. But it certainly was still, in my view, democratic and at different levels. The -- there were different rules for the Presidency, different rules for the Assembly, and different rules still for the voting in the particular -- in the 109 municipalities of Bosnia. But they were all in the broad sense democratic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So your testimony today is that in Bosnia there weren't any divisions along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very different question. I have not testified to that whatsoever, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please give me an answer. I don't see your answer. Were there any divisions along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you said: "So your testimony today is ..." You're seeking confirmation of what you consider to be the testimony of the witness today, and by saying "that's a very different question. I have not testified to that whatsoever, no." It's a clear "no" answer to your question. That is not what Mr. -- or the witness says he testified to today, and you couldn't be surprised by that answer if you have carefully listened to his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I listened to the testimony of this witness very carefully all the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm not seeking any further comments from you. I think I was clear enough and I already -- before you insisted on an answer you had got already, I said - which I hardly ever say - "next question, please, Mr. Lukic."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, today in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Assembly and in the Presidency, are the same systems in place, systems of protection for the three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim, Croat, and Serb peoples, as was the case in the communist times, as you called them. Is it correct that the Dayton Agreement and the Dayton constitution gives the same guarantee and the same protection to each and every people, through the institute of protecting vital national interest?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say they are similar, but not the same. The protection is not as absolute in the Dayton constitution, if you will, as it was in the -- in socialist provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this protection is now part of the Presidency as well, not only in the Assembly, which had not been the case earlier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're drawing me into an area that I'm not terribly familiar with. I'm just hesitant. It would be a speculative answer. I'm sorry, I'd rather not answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not invited to speculate. If you don't feel comfortable to answer the question, please tell us and Mr. Lukic will then put his next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're going to abandon this topic and I'm going to ask you this: In your research, did you come across a statement made by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who said that for him a united Bosnia-Herzegovina is more important than peace and that he is prepared to sacrifice peace for the sake of a single Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He made that statement in the context of a longer proclamation in which he expressed his abhorrence of war and noted that for him, as a very last resort, he would resort -- he would sacrifice peace if it was guaranteed to assure a single Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was in February of 1991 in the Assembly of the Bosnian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, what is the difference between the right to secession of Croats and Muslims from Yugoslavia in relation to the right of secession of the Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are both justified or is one justified and the other one unjustified? In that historical context, how do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a -- really a legal question that goes to the interaction between the two constitutions, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, which in turn goes directly to the question whether it's justified or not. And I just can't comment on a legal issue like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see P2001 again. We need page 22 in e-court in English and page 30 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which report is that now, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's report on the Assembly of Republika Srpska. And it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you refer to the item, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's two pages less. It's page 20 in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking the items. They're numbered as items.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 42, 37th Session on 10th of January, 1994. It's the last paragraph on this page in English and it's on the middle of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see here that President Karadzic already in the beginning of 1994 mentions that the territory held by Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina will possibly go down by 50 per cent. In your research, what sources did you get to or what conclusion did you reach? When did the international community decide that the division in Bosnia should be 51 to 49 per cent, 51 per cent for the Muslims and Croats and 49 per cent for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, just one moment, I believe the translation in English came through that it was down by 50 per cent. I think that we all agree it went down to 50 per cent in the territory of Bosnia. And this occurred after the -- about the time that the Contact Group plan came into play when the Bosnian government and -- it's actually was in the debates and the Bosnian parliament found that there was strong opposition to the Owen-Stoltenberg plan because it only gave about I think 30 per cent of the land to Muslims, to the -- to the Bosnian government side. And so after that, the -- this percentage game that the international community wanted to play resulted in the notion of approximately slightly less than 50 per cent to go to the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the documentation that you studied, would you agree that after that period a time of constant pressure against the Serb side started to agree to 49 per cent and that that is the time when the international community openly sided with the Muslims and Croats in this war in order to achieve that balance of 49/51 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your view would not change even if you knew that representatives of UNPROFOR confirmed this question of mine?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- wanted to see that they had, in fact, confirmed it as you asked it, and frankly it wouldn't change my opinion here. In view of the big picture, I don't think the -- that change that you're talking about really took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the war in Bosnia actually a war for territories?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The other two peoples in BH, did they want to control as large a part of the territory as possible too?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've established that the Serbs did not want to control as large a part of the territory as possible, that their goals were quite specific, they were ambitious but not as large as possible. And I don't believe that the objectives of the other two peoples were either. The -- it's questionable whether the Muslims as a people or the representatives who claimed to be representatives of the Muslim people really had such goals. They favoured a unitary Bosnia which didn't recognise these kinds of distinctions. But certainly the Croats did not have that kind of ambition, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Croats at the time, did they also aspire for a separate state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of their leaders did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's look at page 33 in e-court now of your report, that's the English version, and page 44 in Serbian. It is number 72. It is probably page 31 in your report itself. You're talking here about a homogenous relocation of refugees. The person who has the same name as I do, Mr. Lukic, says the following: We succeeded in carrying out the homogenous relocation of refugees in the beginning of war. Which refugees is he talking about here, the Serb refugees or the refugees from another ethnic community? How do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear. It could pertain to all -- refugees of all groups or only to one or two. Just not clear in this passage what he is referring to. I think he's referring to the broad process of relocating refugees rather than -- he's very likely referring to the broad process rather than anything specific to one group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to conduct a homogenous relocation to somebody else's territory and to put people from another area in one place in another's territory? It seems obvious that here we are talking about Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- that question presupposes that you have fixed boundaries and established areas. And I think if you assume that context, then I think the answer to your question is: No, you can't do that. However, he's speaking about the beginning of the war at a time when boundaries either didn't exist or were being formed, that is, boundaries between areas of control by the various factions, and in some cases were very porous. So I don't know that that really helps us clarify the likely referent here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never talked to Mr. Lukic and you never asked him what he meant by this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only actually have spoken with one Mr. Lukic and he's in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let us briefly look at page 66 in English and 89 in the B/C/S. It should be 64 and the item is 155. As we can see, at the session of 24th March 1992 President Karadzic is saying the following: The policemen have been forced out of the municipalities of Stari Grad, Gorazde, and I think from Visegrad as well. "Milicioneri" means "policemen," can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What can you infer from this text? Who is throwing or forcing out whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was of course Karadzic's position that the Bosnian government police, police loyal to the unified MUP, were throwing out Serbs. I think the reality on the ground, the evidence suggests, was much more mixed. The first actual division of a police station that I know of took place in Bosanska Krupa in early September of 1991, and in that circumstance local SDS leaders actually led the Serb policemen out of the station of the joint -- the unified MUP to another village nearby and established a separate Serb police station. The situation in Stari Grad and in -- and in Pale was complex and actually kind of contested. The process seems to have been started on about the 2nd of March, 1992, at the time of the barricades when some of the Serbian policemen from the Stari Grad station participated in the actual manning of the barricades and thereafter ceased to come to work in the Stari Grad station. So it's a mixed picture, I would say, in terms of who initiated these things, although it clearly was Karadzic's position here and he expressed it on many other occasions that all of this was initiated by the government side and expelled Serb policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is this what you wanted to ask the witness, the -- whether what Mr. Karadzic describes is what happened in the municipalities he mentioned, whether that was the overall picture? Is that what you wanted to -- because it was unclear to me whether that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it was overall picture at that time as well, only here we have some concrete examples --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you ask, "What can you infer from this text?" The text says our policemen are thrown out in the three municipalities he mentioned, and then -- the question was: What can you infer from this ... ? What you wanted to know whether that was representative for what happened everywhere? Is that -- what was your question? I'm just guessing about what you were asking the witness. I've heard his answer. If that's what you wanted to ask him, then no problem; if it's not then I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify first these three stations but I don't think I got the answer I envisaged and I would like to pursue a bit more on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked him who was thrown out. I think the witness answered that in those three instances. Karadzic referred to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know the specific situation in Gorazde in Visegrad, so I can only say the final result was that pure Serb police force took over there, but I don't know how that happened. I do in the case of Stari Grad, as I indicated, try to give you some feel for those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you gave a bit of an overall picture being very mixed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's what you wanted to know, Mr. Lukic -- otherwise, try to focus your questions such a way that you get answers to the questions you put.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say government forces or the forces loyal to the government, are you primarily referring to Muslims when you say that and an occasional Croat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it again depends on the period. At the very beginning of the war from 1991 until sometime in, let's say, I think March of 1992, there were, in fact, two very closely co-operating heads of MUP, I think it was Delimustafic and a Serb whose name I can't remember right now. So I mean, they worked very closely, I thought, to try to keep MUP unified and of course in the long run failed. And after that period of time it was indeed primarily Muslims who made up the MUP which organisationally was the same one that had existed prior to 19 -- prior to April 1992, but owing to the Serb withdrawal as ordered on May 30th -- or, I'm sorry, March 30th was almost completely devoid of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This division is by no means a democratic one. It's a division along ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're -- the -- that's not a dichotomy. It was not democratic in the sense that it was accomplished, at least in part, by force. And it, in the end, produced a largely ethnic division between the police -- the MUP of the Republika Srpska on the one hand and the MUP or the police of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the role of General Mladic at these Assembly sessions? Was he entitled to pass any decisions or to vote for anything or was he merely allowed to make proposals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, he was a guest and didn't have a right to vote, for that matter didn't even really have a right to formally make a proposal. There was a lot of flexibility, particularly in the earlier sessions, of the Assembly in which the guest came to number in the tens and often took the liberty of making proposals and even voting. So it's not inconceivable that he may have at some point actually engaged in those activities, but I don't know that he ever did. He was, I think, an influential voice, making suggestions, advocating policies, and engaging in the discussions about those policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 79 in e-court, paragraph 2, 107 and paragraph 1 in the B/C/S - and I'm talking about your paper - it's item 185 under number 2, or rather, the paragraph that begins with "secondly," we see that General Mladic is seeking a state of war to be proclaimed. So we are talking about the session held on the 12th of May, 1992. You would agree that the state of war was not proclaimed and that this proposal of General Mladic went unheeded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could I possibly implore the usher to refill my water. I think the ushers have inadvertently engaged in the policy of separation of the water and the glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All of us are here pressurised by time and space. Doctor, I had quite a few more questions but I promised the Chamber and you that I would finish during the first session. I am sorry to have been a burden to you, and at this point I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's been no burden, Mr. Lukic. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I establish, Mr. Lukic, that you finished even before the end of the first session this morning. Ms. Bibles, do you have any further questions for Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would they take approximately?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No more than 15 minutes and perhaps considerably less than that. I could -- I'll certainly get started before the break and may finish by the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's get started. If you feel that at 10.30 you would need no more than five minutes, please indicate so that we could consider to take the break slightly later; but if it would be seven, eight, or more minutes then we'll take the break anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: First I want to go back to a matter that I need to clarify with respect to P2001 relating to highlights 258 and 259. I believe you corrected the date of the 20th Assembly, and I want to make sure that we corrected that to -- to the accurate date. I believe we gave a date in July. Could you give us an accurate date for the 20th Assembly relating to those two highlights?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it was the 16th and 17th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is it possible that would have been the 14th and 15th of September for the 20th Session? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is my recollection. That is obviously not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: To go -- turn full attention now to cross-examination. Last Thursday you were asked questions relating to the transformation of the JNA, and that would be the second section of your Sarajevo report. You were asked some specifics about Kijevo and I'd like to go back to that area. Can you tell us why you used the Kijevo battle in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used it for two reasons: Number one, General Mladic had a very -- well, the leading role in the Serb forces in that battle; and, number two, it is cited by General Mladic himself in Assembly sessions, and also in this wonderful book of interviews that was done with him during the war time by Jovan Janjic, as a seminal event in the evolution of the conflict in both Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could ask the Court Officer to bring P2001, e-court in English page 78 and page 106 in B/C/S and looking at highlight 184.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In looking at highlight 184, is that one of the segments that you were just relating to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of them, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you read -- and this is a segment. Could you review this highlight or read this highlight very quickly for us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read in English: "'The Knin'" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please do it at such a speed of speech that the interpreters can follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wonder if it would be useful to identify it in B/C/S so the translators could use the actual B/C/S that General Mladic used in the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And perhaps, given the time, Your Honours, I would bring attention to the first paragraph specifically of excerpt 184.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And by way of question, who does General Mladic refer to in this first paragraph in that excerpt?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He refers to Milan Martic who was the chief of police, he was the minister of MUP, minister of internal affairs, of the break-away Serb polity in Croatia, the Serb Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And now I'd like to shift direction to a series of questions that you were asked yesterday regarding the nature of the 16th Assembly and the six strategic objectives. You were also asked whether you were aware that Ratko Mladic came to Bosnia on the 9th of May, 1992. Do you recall that line of questions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you aware of any information or evidence that Ratko Mladic was involved in the discussions regarding the strategic objectives prior to the 16th Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a reference in his diary to a meeting which he attended I believe several days before the six strategic goals were laid out by Karadzic on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the Court Officer could bring P00352, which is one of the Mladic notebooks, to our screens. I would ask for e-court page 262 in English and e-court page 270 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We're looking now at -- it appears that we have both versions on the screen now. Could you tell us what we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an enumeration of the, in this case, seven strategic goals in which in the notebook General Mladic attributes these to Mr. Krajisnik. The -- obviously the seven goals do not correspond completely with the six goals that were laid out on the 12th, and in fact the seventh one was the one that was not -- did not -- was not carried forward to the final enunciation. But otherwise they are recognisably those that were laid out on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I believe you have reflected in your testify that he attributes these to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll ask two questions: First, could you briefly tell us what that seventh strategic objective was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To establish links with the RSK, the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that polity within the boundaries of Croatia that lay in Croatia and was a break-away -- as I characterised, a break-away republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us based on your read of this page what other individuals were present -- apparently present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozidar Vucurevic, who was a very prominent SDS leader in western Herzegovina, and Mr. Karadzic, of course, was also present. That's I think the only persons we can determine from this excerpt that were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll ask if we could go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the date of this meeting is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is dated the 7th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And just briefly, are you aware of whether or not there were similar meetings relating to Bosnia on the 6th of May, 1992, reflected in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I recall there was a meeting on the 6th which without enumerating them also discussed the goals to be outlined for the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, at this point I have no further re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have the questions in re-direct triggered the need for any further cross? Then, Mr. Donia, this -- if Mr. Mladic would like to consult then -- because Mr. Donia might be gone if we don't take the opportunity now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems that Mr. Mladic would have some questions based on the re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest the following: That you consult with Mr. Mladic during the break and that you put any additional questions to the witness after the break. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps before we go to break it would be a good time, before Dr. Donia leaves, to move to admit the exhibits P1999, 2000, 2001, and 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they're all MFI'd. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will have the same objections we had before on those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll consider it over the break now having heard the testimony of the witness, at least if I could say 99 per cent of the testimony of the witness, and we'll then decide after the break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We need you for a short while after the break, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, no need to remind you of the limits of the areas to be covered at the present stage of the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's exactly in these limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I've already said that we have no further questions, but I'm coming back with a few. It won't be long. We'll go into a bit of history now. Let's see whether you are familiar with this. Do you know when the Independent State of Croatia was established in 1941 what happened to the Serb population in the village of -- the village of Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specifically -- for Kijevo, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will put something to you. Fifty inhabitants of Kijevo in 1941 were invited to a meeting and they were all killed except for one who managed to escape. You never came across this information? They were killed by Ustasha formations.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across information that the town -- village of Kijevo had been, in fact, the subject of these -- of attacks by the Ustasha and that there were casualties, but I did not go into the specifics. I looked at it only in the broader context of the Ustasha killings of Jews, Serbs, Roma, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when things were happening in 1991 in Kijevo, Mr. Mladic was not commander. He was Chief of Staff of the 9th Corps of the JNA. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- acknowledge that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Spiro Ninkovic was the commander. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're -- you refreshed my memory that that was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, that is to say the time that we are talking about, do you know that the barracks in Sinj, Zadar, Split had all been under a blockade for six months already by then without water, electricity, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've written about in the report and acknowledged in testimony that these blockades existed of various "kasarna" in Croatia. I didn't go into the details about exactly which one were, how long they were, and whether they were totally without water or electricity. So I can't confirm that specifically, but there was no question that a number of those "kasarna" were -- had been isolated and that were under siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I suggest that we -- that you first deal with the questions and then consult with Mr. Mladic, that whatever remains then can be added to your questions, because otherwise it will -- the further examination will be interrupted again and again. You have an opportunity before Mr. Donia will be excused to consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time General Perisic was commander of the barracks in Zadar? Did you come across that information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall coming across that information. I have no reason to dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you come across information to the effect that in the barracks that were under siege people who were killed in the barracks had to be buried in the barracks themselves under floors?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I say, I didn't really go much beyond the fact that they were -- the sieges were established and that there were JNA troops in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, as regards the incident in Kijevo itself, did you come across information to the effect that a corpse, the corpse of Zeljko Vranjes, was supposed to be taken through Kijevo? He was returning home from Switzerland. He was arrested in Vinkovci, taken to Sibenik, beaten for a few days there, until he was killed, and then he was thrown on a dump in Sibenik and he was found there, picked up, and driven through Kijevo in order to be buried in Civljani, his own village?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the time in Kijevo a police station had been established whose komandir was Ante Bajan and that they prevented this column from passing through, the people who were supposed to bury Zeljko Vranjes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of these items that you've mentioned, I have written about and can confirm that a police station was established by the Croatian MUP in Kijevo and that it did engage in -- put up blockades, preventing passage of persons and goods. The rest I do not have any knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you come across information to the effect that it was precisely because of that that Milan Martic was called upon, or rather, the police to resolve the problem with the Croatian MUP and that was the reason why both the policemen and the military took part in this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you come across information that precisely during those days the commander of the barracks in Bjelovar was killed, Rajko Kovacevic, a lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know the name. There were certainly -- certainly casualties at that time in a low-level sniping and shooting that was going on, but I don't know specifically the names of the individual casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second. I just have to consult with the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Low volume and I hear it even through my earphones. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, on the 19th of September, did you know that a column had been attacked, a column that was withdrawing from the Karlovac barracks? And the leader of the column had his throat slit and all the soldiers were killed. That happened at Koranski Most, the Korana bridge, on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Thank you for your answers. This is indeed the end of your examination now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I can confirm that, Mr. -- Low volume, only a very short consultation. I confirmed ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I can ask for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no more questions, Mr. Lukic. The last question you put to the witness after having consulted with Mr. Mladic resulted in an answer that the witness didn't know. So that can -- the lack of knowledge of the witness cannot have triggered any need for further questions. So we leave it to that. Mr. Donia -- Mr. -- no, Mr. Mladic, we'll now first excuse Mr. Donia before we continue. Mr. Donia, I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague. You know the route by now I take it, and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And you are excused. I wish you a safe return home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's been an honour to be before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber will decide on the admission of P1999, P2000, P2001, and P2002. All four are admitted into evidence. And, Mr. Lukic, the Chamber has also considered that during your examination of the witness you have extensively used portions of that evidence as well. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are four additional items or exhibits that I would move to tender from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to this witness, that's -- one second. Ms. Bibles, if we take them one by one the first one would be ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 03189, is that on your -- 03189, speech by Karadzic November 1991. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2005. Next one, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff operational directive dated the 25th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2006, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: VRS Main Staff addition to directive number 4 dated 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2007, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that last one, Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Speech of Major-General Dragomir Milosevic, ceremony of presenting war flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2008, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2005 through P2008, all four are admitted. There's no need to have them under seal, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: One final matter, Your Honour. Mr. Lukic -- I would like to have an opportunity to speak with Mr. Lukic about sections of the assembly minutes which have been described in the testimony today, where perhaps we need more of the assembly session than the excerpts that were presented. I would suggest that one we have an opportunity to discuss these in a little more depth that we would then present them to the Trial Chamber either in writing or we could return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if both parties would agree on adding excerpts beyond what is presented by Mr. Donia, then of course the Chamber will hear of that and will likely follow such a suggestion. Nothing else, Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: May I be excused, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused. For the next witness, no protective measures. Will it be you, Ms. Harbour, who will examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any matters we have to pay attention to before he enters the courtroom? I don't think so. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And that will be Mr. Turkusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Turkusic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Turkusic, you'll first be examined by Ms. Harbour. Ms. Harbour is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll find her to your right. You may proceed, Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Emir Turkusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You previously testified in the trials of Dragomir Milosevic, Momcilo Perisic, and Radovan Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And you've also given several statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to review an amalgamated statement containing relevant information from your prior testimonies and statements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter number 30183, which is a statement dated 19 July 2013 be placed on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Turkusic, do you recognise the document that is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: This document is the amalgamated statement that I recently signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And the signature at the bottom of the page, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And if we could please go to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity prior to testifying today to review this statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read it in its entirety, in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You identified several corrections that need to be made to this document, and I'm going to go through those with you now. At paragraph 17 of the statement it currently states: "Both errors lead to a delay in impulse after firing ..." This should instead read: "Both errors lead to a change in impulse after firing ..." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: At paragraph 36 in your comment related to the first document, the B/C/S original of this statement states that "the projectile originated from the south-west." This should be changed to "south-east"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In paragraph 47 it refers to a number KV9405. This should instead refer to KV9404; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In paragraph 50 the reference to "south-west" should be changed to "south-east"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In paragraph 65 halfway through the paragraph is a sentence that reads: "And then you have alpha degree and that is on what our calculation is based." And you would like to clarify that this sentence should instead read: "And then you can calculate the alpha angle." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And for the final correction that you identified, if we could go to paragraph 117, in your comment related to 65 ter 15718 you refer to the signatures of yourself and Nedim Bosnic. This should refer to initials and not to signatures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the report I have it says already "initials." So I'm talking about -- let me just have a look. Paragraph 117, last item: "This is my report and I recognise my initials and those ..." That's what I have in my hard copy. Then apparently there are two versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I believe I can clarify the issue. In the original 92 ter filing we attached a provisional translation which was subsequently revised. In the revision process, since it had to be consistent with the original Bosnian statement, the word "signature" was changed to "initials," and now the witness would like to correct that to reflect that it should indeed be "initials." And the revised translation was distributed about a little over a week ago, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that revised version was attached to the 92 ter motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The version attached to the 92 ter motion was the unrevised translation, and in the meantime as of approximately a week and a half ago the revised version has become available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will sort this out and -- Ms. Harbour. Because what I was provided with is a version which contains already all this, so we'll check carefully what was attached to the 92 ter motion. Perhaps I received already a more recent one, but it's clear at least what the testimony of the witness is in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Turkusic, with these changes if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked in preparation for this statement would you give the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the accuracy of the truthfulness of this statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. I confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to tender 65 ter 30183, which is this amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the same objections we had in our motion filed on the 9th of August, 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you just remind me exactly what the basis of the objections ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have that motion with me since I have only documents from Dr. Donia with me. I'll have it in a couple minutes probably, but I know that we mainly objected to the expert nature of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be MFI'd. Under what number, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 30183 will be MFI P2009, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are 37 associated exhibits for this statement which have not yet been admitted into evidence. Ms. Stewart has supplied the Chamber and the Registry and the parties with this list via e-mail. Thirty-three of these documents have never been assigned exhibit numbers and four have been marked not admitted and we would tender all of those 37 exhibits pursuant to Rule 92 ter as inseparable and indispensable parts of the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that at this very moment that Mr. Registrar, having received the list, will provisionally assign numbers and that we will then decide at the end of the examination of the witness about admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if there's any question about whether any of these exhibits are inseparable and indispensable to the witness's statement, I would request to be informed at this stage, while the witness is still on the stand, so that I can address and tender the documents through the witness rather than leaving them to a separate mechanism of tendering at a later stage. And although I've planned only a small number of questions for the witness, I would use additional time as necessary to ensure that each of these associated exhibits are admitted into evidence. And in the alternative, we would request the Chamber to admit these documents pursuant to Rule 89(C), as the witness statement provides information establishing both relevance and authenticity for each document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Okay. I would now like to read a public summary of the 92 ter evidence of this witness and I've explained the purpose of this summary to the witness. Dr. Turkusic was a member of the counter-sabotage protection unit of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was known as the KDZ, in 1994 and 1995. The witness and his team conducted numerous ballistic investigations into shelling incidents in Sarajevo. He provides evidence of the KDZ's role in shelling investigations, the method of determining the direction of fire of a mortar round, the accuracy of mortars, and the nature of modified air-bombs. He discusses in detail investigative documentation relating to many shelling incidents. His team was responsible for determining the type of projectile that was used in these incidents. He was involved in analysing the craters caused by mortar impacts and was also involved in identifying and analysing projectile fragments gathered at various crime scenes. The witness can attest to the significance of markings found on some of these fragments, most notably the markings found on mortar stabiliser fins which revealed that they were manufactured in Krusik Valjevo in Serbia and the year and the month. Dr. Turkusic testifies in particular about the Markale II shelling incident on the 28th of August, 1995, in which a 120-millimetre mortar shell detonated outside the entrance to the city market. This is scheduled incident G18. Dr. Turkusic describes the atmosphere of panic and fear at the incident site. He notes the stabiliser of the projectile bore markings which indicated that it was manufactured in Valjevo, Serbia, in July 1993. He explains that the 120-millimetre mortar round is an anti-personnel projectile, designed to destroy manpower. It sprays its shrapnel in a horizontal fashion close to the ground. Dr. Turkusic discusses the minimal possible angle of descent and the direction of fire of the projectile. He also provides evidence about four other shelling incidents impacting close to the city market around the same time as the Markale II shelling, using mortars bearing the same Krusik Valjevo markings. And this concludes the public summary. Your Honours, I now have a few questions for this witness and in addition if there is dispute about the inseparability and indispensability of the documents, I will go through any documents that may not be admitted as associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear from Mr. Lukic later. So if it would be possible to -- do you have any questions which are not affected by our judgement on inseparability and --

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: The report was compiled by Ekrem Suljevic who was a member of our unit and he signed it. My comment about the fact that it was an UTU fuse was based on the conclusion of my colleague in view of the type of the shell and the effect of its exploding immediately and causing an undelayed explosion, that the fuse was mounted at the top of the shell, shape-charged shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: So if you could just -- I'm not sure that that's completely clear. If you could just tell us what is a UTU M62 fuse?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: It's a fuse which is placed at the top of the shell and it is adjustable so that it causes instantaneous explosion at the slightest touch. It can also be adjusted so that it has a delayed effect by programming a relative unknown period of delay of explosion of the shell to allow it for the shell to penetrate the surface. So that is the delayed fuse which are activated when you want to destroy some fortifications or penetrate through an obstacle as opposed to the fuse which is activated immediately on impact and which are always used to destroy manpower because the explosion takes place immediately upon contact with the surface.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: During an investigation, how would you be able to tell if a -- an immediate contact fuse was used?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: According to the traces on the hard surface, if the surface was a hard one, its main explosive effect and the dispersion of shrapnel happened at the point of impact with the surface, and the effects are recognisable by the fact that in three-dimensional geometry of space the place of explosion can be recognisable and an indisputable conclusion can be reached that the explosion took place immediately at the moment of contact with the surface.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And how would you be able to tell in an investigation if a delayed fuse was used instead?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: So if the effect of the explosion is such that it causes a penetration of the location or an obstacle that one wishes to destroy, we can see an in-depth effect of explosion resulting in destruction of an embankment or any other obstacle and its devastating effect deep under the place of explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And would it be possible for a contact -- an immediate contact fuse to embed in the ground?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: The body of the shell fuse is made of aluminum. It is a very light and soft metal. At impacting hard surface, it become completely deformed and only small pieces of it can be found. So in the proximity of the centre of explosion it is very soft and usually become completely destroyed; however, it is possible sometimes to find some pieces depending on the explosion and depending on the surface on which the shell fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, could I ask clarification of one of the previous answers, whether I understood it well or not. I read from one of your answers, and it is about a delayed fuse. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it is essentially the same because there are many possible obstacles in view of their mechanical qualities. However, if the contact with the surface happened instantaneously, then in depth in the soil there is no such trace. It is a well-known thing that instantaneous shells, when they fall into tree-tops, they are activated immediately when they impact the tree-top. It does -- there is no in-depth effect.
